LePlanner: An Iterative Amortized Controller For World Models

Saksham Bansal1*, Om Naphade2*, Chayan Aggarwal3*, Vrishin M4
1Department of Mechanical Engineering, 2Department of Physics, 3Department of Mathematics, 4Department of Chemical Engineering
Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee
{saksham_b@me, om_nn@ph, chayan_a@ma, vrishin_m@ch}.iitr.ac.in
Abstract

World models trained with joint-embedding predictive architectures learn compact, structured latent manifolds from physical interaction, yet planning in those latents still relies on one of two costly families of methods. Search-based planners (CEM, MPPI, iCEM) optimize action sequences through many predictor rollouts, achieving strong success at the price of high per-decision compute and latency. Policy-based methods (behavior cloning, GC-IDM) amortize inference into a single forward pass, but degrade on contact-rich tasks where the demonstration distribution is multi-modal. Neither family offers both low latency and robust goal-reaching in a learned latent space. We propose LePlanner, an amortized iterative controller that refines latent action sequences to reach a goal state, trained with an arrival–hold loss that rewards reaching the goal at the earliest feasible horizon and staying there, plus an action gaussian loss which keeps actions in their true manifold. Across goal-directed environments spanning navigation, contact-rich manipulation, and continuous control, LePlanner matches or exceeds the success of test-time search planners while requiring an order-of-magnitude fewer predictor invocations and 33–49×49\times lower wall-clock per decision. We report 98%98\% on PushT, 100%100\% on Reacher, 100%100\% on TwoRooms, and 92%92\% on the ogbench cube. The results show that, in a sufficiently regularized latent space, much of the structure that search discovers online can be amortized into a lightweight learned iterative policy, yielding fast, horizon-aware, nonlinear physical control without online optimization.

1 Introduction

A central goal of artificial intelligence is to develop agents that learn useful behavior across diverse tasks and environments directly from observations (Levine et al., 2016). World models are one promising approach: they learn to predict how an environment state evolves in response to an action, so agents can evaluate possible action sequences before executing them, effectively planning inside a learned model of the world (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2019). Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) learn such models in a compact latent space rather than predicting every detail of future observations, which works particularly well when the observation channel is high dimensional (LeCun, 2022; Assran et al., 2023; Sobal et al., 2022). Recent work on LeWorldModel (LeWM) demonstrated that a JEPA based world model can be trained stably from raw pixels while supporting efficient visual control (Maes et al., 2026).

Planning through a learned world model forces a three-way choice: search-based planners (ie. CEM) are accurate but costly and high-latency, solving a full optimization loop at every decision (Rubinstein, 1999; Chua et al., 2018; Hafner et al., 2019); cloning-based policies (GC-IDM) amortize inference into a single forward pass but degrade on contact-rich and nonlinear tasks where the demonstration distribution is poorly conditioned (Nguyen et al., 2026); and model-based policy methods (TDMPC2) train the controller inside the world model’s imagination, coupling the policy to a task-specific dynamics model that demands substantial compute to train on real environments and can struggle with complex long-horizon structure (Hansen et al., 2024).

We also find that a conventional terminal objective used in such controllers creates a rather subtle failure when deployed in a varied receding-horizon setting (Mayne et al., 2000). The objective trains the controller to reach the goal at the end of its planning horizon. When deployed, only the first part of the plan is executed before replanning, which resets the terminal deadline, so the controller repeatedly approaches the goal while postponing actual arrival in many cases. We refer to this behavior as horizon-reset procrastination.

To resolve this mismatch and to bring the cost of non-amortized controllers down, we propose LePlanner, an amortized controller that learns to construct and iteratively refine action plans through a frozen LeWM predictor (Srinivas et al., 2018; Marino et al., 2018), trained with an arrival-and-hold objective. During training, the controller is supervised to reach the goal at the temporal offset from which that goal was sampled, rather than at the fixed end of every plan, and is then encouraged to remain near the goal for the rest of the predicted trajectory. The temporal offset is used only to define the training loss and is never provided to the controller at inference, so the method requires no modification to the frozen world model or controller architecture. In the currently recorded PushT evaluation, LePlanner reaches 98%98\% success while replanning after every action block: the corrected objective removes the procrastination behavior and allows the controller to use frequent replanning without repeatedly deferring the goal. LePlanner also achieves high success rate in evaluations such as TwoRoom and Reacher.

2 Related Work

Latent world models and visual planning.

World models learn predictive representations that allow agents to reason about the consequences of their actions before acting (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018). Early latent world-model approaches either optimized action sequences online, as in PlaNet (Hafner et al., 2019), or jointly learned task-oriented latent dynamics and terminal values for model-predictive control (Hansen et al., 2022). Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures instead predict future latent representations rather than reconstructing observations (LeCun, 2022; Assran et al., 2023), and DINO-based models show that self-supervised vision features yield smooth latent spaces suitable for downstream control (Caron et al., 2021; Oquab et al., 2024). This principle has been extended to action-conditioned latent dynamics (Sobal et al., 2022) and to planning over frozen visual representations (Zhou et al., 2025). LeWorldModel learns an action-conditioned JEPA end-to-end from pixels and provides the frozen world model used in our work (Maes et al., 2026). Recent studies improve latent planning by reducing the mismatch between world-model training and planning (Parthasarathy et al., 2025), or by regularizing latent trajectories to improve the geometry of the planning objective (Wang et al., 2026). Our work is complementary: we keep the learned representation and dynamics fixed and study how the controller’s training objective interacts with receding-horizon execution.

Planning in latent worlds: search, cloning, and learned policies.

Planning over a learned world model is most often done by test-time search. The cross-entropy method (CEM) (Rubinstein, 1999) and MPPI (Williams et al., 2017) optimize action sequences by iteratively refining a distribution over candidate plans through the learned dynamics, and PETS (Chua et al., 2018) combines such sampling with probabilistic ensembles; iCEM adds implicit differentiation for continuous refinement. These search planners achieve strong success but repeat substantial computation at each decision, evaluating hundreds to thousands of latent rollouts per step. An alternative is to amortize planning into a learned policy: goal-conditioned behavior cloning (GCBC) and Goal-Conditioned Inverse Dynamics Models (GC-IDM) map a current latent state, goal latent, and horizon directly to the next action (Nguyen et al., 2026). Because they are trained purely on demonstration data, such policies amortize inference into a single forward pass but degrade on contact-rich or multi-modal tasks where the behavioral cloning distribution is poorly conditioned. A third family trains policies inside the world model’s imagination: Dreamer (Hafner et al., 2020; Hafner et al., 2024) trains an actor-critic entirely on imagined latent rollouts, and TDMPC2 (Hansen et al., 2024) extends this with joint latent-reward learning and TD-planning over short imagination horizons. Our controller bridges these families. Like search planners it reasons through the learned dynamics over multiple horizons; like amortized policies it performs a fixed number of learned refinements at deployment; and like model-based policy methods it trains the controller end-to-end – but over a frozen, task-agnostic world model, with an explicit arrival-and-hold objective.

Amortized and iterative inference.

Iterative amortized inference combines a learned initial prediction with repeated learned corrections (Marino et al., 2018), and Universal Planning Networks (Srinivas et al., 2018) learn representations in which plans are optimized through differentiable latent rollouts. More broadly, iterative refinement underlies energy-based models (LeCun et al., 2006) and consistency models (Song et al., 2023). Our controller follows this amortized formulation, but unlike online CEM the search procedure is learned during training, and unlike Universal Planning Networks the world model is pretrained and frozen and the controller is not trained by imitating expert action sequences. This separation lets us change the controller objective without changing the underlying visual representation or dynamics.

3 Method: LePlanner

We consider offline, visual, goal-conditioned control using a pretrained and frozen latent world model. Our objective is to learn a controller that produces action plans from an observation history and a goal image, without imitating the actions in the offline dataset.

3.1 Problem setting

Let an offline trajectory be τ=(o0,a0,o1,a1,…)\tau=(o_{0},a_{0},o_{1},a_{1},\ldots), where oto_{t} is a visual observation and at∈ℝdaa_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}} is an environment action. We use a pretrained LeWorldModel (LeWM) (Maes et al., 2026), consisting of an image encoder E:ot↦zt∈ℝDE:o_{t}\mapsto z_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} and an action-conditioned latent predictor PP. Environment actions are grouped into blocks of ff consecutive actions; a block is denoted by bj∈ℝAb_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{A}, where A=f​daA=fd_{a}. At time tt, the controller receives NN context latents Ct=(zt−N+1,…,zt)C_{t}=(z_{t-N+1},\ldots,z_{t}), the N−1N-1 action blocks connecting these observations, and a goal latent zG=E⁡(oG)z_{G}=E(o_{G}). It produces a plan b1:H=(b1,…,bH)b_{1:H}=(b_{1},\ldots,b_{H}) of HH future action blocks. Given a candidate plan, the frozen predictor generates an autoregressive latent rollout:

z^1:H=ℛP(Ct,bt−N+1:t−1,b1:H),\hat{z}_{1:H}=\mathcal{R}_{P}\left(C_{t},b_{t-N+1:t-1},b_{1:H}\right), (1)

where ℛP\mathcal{R}_{P} applies PP using the same sliding observation and action history used during world-model training. We measure the predicted distance to the goal after block jj as dj=1D​∥z^j−zG∥22d_{j}=\tfrac{1}{D}\lVert\hat{z}_{j}-z_{G}\rVert_{2}^{2}. The parameters of EE and PP remain frozen throughout controller training. The cached outputs of EE are treated as data, while gradients are retained through the operations of PP so that the controller can learn how its proposed actions affect the predicted trajectory.

3.2 LePlanner

LePlanner amortizes trajectory optimization into a fixed number of learned refinement steps. It maintains one hidden plan token yj∈ℝWy_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{W} for each future action block, Y(k)=(y1(k),…,yH(k))Y^{(k)}=(y_{1}^{(k)},\ldots,y_{H}^{(k)}), where kk denotes the refinement iteration. The context latents and goal latent are projected into the controller width and augmented with learned positional and role embeddings; these conditioning tokens are read by every refinement step. The initial plan is produced from learned plan queries, Y(0)=Gθ​([Q;𝟎],Ct,zG)Y^{(0)}=G_{\theta}([Q;\mathbf{0}],C_{t},z_{G}), where QQ contains one learned query per plan position and the zero argument indicates that no predicted consequences are available for the initial proposal. An action head hθh_{\theta} decodes every plan token into a bounded action block, bj(k)=ca+sa⊙tanh⁡(hθ​(yj(k)))b_{j}^{(k)}=c_{a}+s_{a}\odot\tanh(h_{\theta}(y_{j}^{(k)})), where cac_{a} and sas_{a} transform the raw action bounds into the normalized action space used by LeWM, so the tanh\tanh parameterization enforces the environment action bounds without clipping.

For each refinement, the decoded plan is rolled through the frozen predictor using Equation (1). For plan position jj, LePlanner constructs the consequence feature uj(k)=[,yj(k);z^j(k);z^j(k)−zG;dj(k),]u_{j}^{(k)}=[,y_{j}^{(k)};\ \hat{z}_{j}^{(k)};\ \hat{z}_{j}^{(k)}-z_{G};\ d_{j}^{(k)},]. A consequence encoder FθF_{\theta} interprets these features jointly with the observation and goal conditioning, and a refinement transformer GθG_{\theta} then predicts a correction for all plan tokens, which updates the plan through a learned step size:

R(k)\displaystyle R^{(k)} =Fθ​(U(k),Ct,zG),\displaystyle=F_{\theta}\!\left(U^{(k)},C_{t},z_{G}\right), V(k)\displaystyle\qquad V^{(k)} =[Y(k);R(k)],\displaystyle=\left[Y^{(k)};R^{(k)}\right], (2)
Δ​Y(k)\displaystyle\Delta Y^{(k)} =Gθ​(V(k),Ct),\displaystyle=G_{\theta}\!\left(V^{(k)},C_{t}\right), Y(k+1)\displaystyle Y^{(k+1)} =Y(k)+σ⁡(ηk)​Δ​Y(k).\displaystyle=Y^{(k)}+\sigma(\eta_{k})\Delta Y^{(k)}.

for k=0,…,K−1k=0,\ldots,K-1, where V(k)V^{(k)} is the concatenation of the current plan and predicted consequences, and σ⁡(ηk)∈(0,1)\sigma(\eta_{k})\in(0,1) and one scalar step size is learned for each refinement. Both FθF_{\theta} and GθG_{\theta} are shared across all KK iterations, so increasing the refinement depth increases inference computation but does not introduce new parameters. The refinement transformer (GθG_{\theta}) applies full self-attention across all HH plan positions before any action block is committed, allowing early and late parts of the plan to be revised jointly.

3.3 Arrival-and-hold objective

A training example is constructed by sampling a future observation from the same offline trajectory as the current context. Let q∈{1,…,H}q\in\{1,\ldots,H\} be the number of world-model transitions between the current observation and this hindsight-relabeled goal (Andrychowicz et al., 2017). The dataset therefore provides not only the goal latent zGz_{G}, but also the offset at which that goal occurs. A fixed-terminal objective would always penalize dHd_{H}, regardless of the sampled offset qq; under receding-horizon execution, this attaches arrival to the end of the repeatedly reset plan. Instead, LePlanner evaluates the predicted trajectory at the goal’s data-derived offset:

ℒAH(k)=dq(k)⏟arrival+λh​1H−q​∑j=q+1Hdj(k)⏟hold,\mathcal{L}^{(k)}_{\mathrm{AH}}=\underbrace{d_{q}^{(k)}}_{\text{arrival}}+\lambda_{h}\underbrace{\frac{1}{H-q}\sum_{j=q+1}^{H}d_{j}^{(k)}}_{\text{hold}}, (3)

where the hold term is defined as zero when q=Hq=H. The arrival term asks the predicted plan to reach the goal at the temporal offset from which the goal was sampled, and the hold term discourages trajectories that briefly pass through the goal and then move away. Importantly, qq is used only to index the training loss; it is never included in the controller input. At inference, LePlanner receives only the observation history and goal, and must infer an appropriate plan without access to a deadline.

3.4 Deep supervision across refinements

LePlanner produces an initial plan followed by KK refined plans, and we supervise every one of these K+1K+1 predictions:

ℒref=∑k=0Kρk​ℒAH(k)∑k=0Kρk,ρk=2k.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ref}}=\frac{\sum_{k=0}^{K}\rho_{k}\mathcal{L}^{(k)}_{\mathrm{AH}}}{\sum_{k=0}^{K}\rho_{k}},\qquad\rho_{k}=2^{k}. (4)

Later refinements receive larger weights, while every intermediate plan retains a direct gradient signal. This makes the initial prediction useful on its own and trains each application of the shared refinement operator rather than supervising only its final output.

3.5 Constraining plans to offline support

Optimizing actions through a learned world model can exploit inaccuracies outside the action distribution represented in the offline data (Fujimoto et al., 2019; Kumar et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2020; Kidambi et al., 2020). We therefore fit a conditional Gaussian mixture density βψ​(b∣C)\beta_{\psi}(b\mid C) to real action blocks and their latent contexts, trained separately and frozen before LePlanner training. For a candidate action block, we define the normalized negative log density r⁡(C,b)=−1A​log⁡βψ​(b∣C)r(C,b)=-\tfrac{1}{A}\log\beta_{\psi}(b\mid C), and let c95c_{95} be the 9595th percentile of this score on real action blocks. For the refined plans, we apply the one-sided support penalty

ℒsup=1K​H​∑k=1K∑j=1H[max⁡(0,r⁡(Cj(k),bj(k))−c95)]2,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sup}}=\frac{1}{KH}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{j=1}^{H}\left[\max\left(0,r(C_{j}^{(k)},b_{j}^{(k)})-c_{95}\right)\right]^{2}, (5)

where Cj(k)C_{j}^{(k)} is the imagined context preceding block jj. The penalty is zero for action blocks inside the selected support region, so it does not train LePlanner to reproduce a particular demonstrated action; the dataset actions are used only to fit βψ\beta_{\psi} and never serve as controller targets. The complete controller objective is ℒLePlanner=ℒref+λsup​ℒsup\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LePlanner}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ref}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{sup}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sup}}. Only the parameters of LePlanner are optimized; the LeWM encoder, LeWM predictor, and behavior-density model remain frozen.

3.6 Receding-horizon execution

At deployment, LePlanner encodes the current observation history and goal, constructs its initial plan, and performs KK learned refinements. No gradient computation or online parameter update is required, and the final plan b1:H(K)b_{1:H}^{(K)} is returned to the environment policy. We use receding-horizon execution: the policy executes a prefix of the plan, observes the resulting state, and invokes LePlanner again (Mayne et al., 2000). The main closed-loop configuration executes one action block before replanning. Thus, the world model remains inside the inference loop, but population-based trajectory search is replaced by a fixed number of amortized refinements.

4 Results

We evaluate LePlanner against three families of latent planners: test-time search (CEM, MPPI, iCEM, gradient optimisation), amortised policies trained by goal-conditioned cloning (GCBC, GCIQL, GCIVL, GC-IDM), and latent world models evaluated with their own planners (PLDM, DINO-WM, LeWM, Fast-LeWM). The four benchmark environments are PushT (Chi et al., 2023), Reacher, TwoRooms, and the OGBench cube task (Park et al., 2025).

4.1 Goal-reaching success

Figure 3 reports success on the four LeWM benchmark environments. LePlanner reaches 100%100\% on TwoRooms, 94%94\% on PushT, 100%100\% on Reacher, and 92%92\% on OGBench-Cube. Against the matched CEM baseline run under an identical protocol, it improves success on every environment we measured. Two properties are worth stating before the numbers are read. First, LePlanner is close to flat in mm, the number of action blocks executed before replanning (100→100100\rightarrow 100 on TwoRooms, 94→8894\rightarrow 88 on PushT, 100→100100\rightarrow 100 on Reacher, 82→9282\rightarrow 92 on Cube), the signature of a time-consistent closed-loop policy rather than a good open-loop one. Second, CEM is not flat: on PushT it moves 34→9034\rightarrow 90 between m=1m{=}1 and m=5m{=}5, so a single receding horizon cannot summarise it, and we report both throughout.

4.2 The cost of a decision

Success alone does not separate an amortised planner from a search planner; the separation is in what a decision costs. We compare LePlanner against CEM only, because these are the two arms we timed on the same GPU, in the same session, against the same trials. Figure 4 reports wall-clock seconds per episode, while predictor rows measure how often the world model is queried. The architectural ratio is exact and independent of hardware: LePlanner issues (K+1)⋅H=4×5=20(K{+}1)\cdot H=4\times 5=20 latent transitions per plan, where CEM issues 300×30×5=45,000300\times 30\times 5=45{,}000, a factor of 22502250. That derived ratio matches the independently measured per-episode row ratio at matched execution.

4.3 What each family requires

Success and latency do not capture the requirement that most constrains deployment: what a method needs in order to be trained and run at all. Table 1 makes those requirements explicit, and two entries deserve comment. The cloning family — GCBC, GCIQL, GCIVL and GC-IDM — regresses directly onto demonstrated actions; GC-IDM minimises ∥GC-IDMψ​(zt,zt+h,h)−at∥22\lVert\text{GC-IDM}_{\psi}(z_{t},z_{t+h},h)-a_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2} over triples drawn from the offline data, so its supervision target is the dataset action and its quality is bounded by the demonstrations. LePlanner never uses a dataset action as a target: they enter only through the frozen density βψ\beta_{\psi}, which bounds the support region (Section 3.5) and contributes exactly zero loss for any plan already inside it. Second, GC-IDM requires the remaining budget at test time, since its control law evaluates ht=T−t+1h_{t}=T-t+1 with TT known in advance, whereas LePlanner is supervised at the offset qq from which each goal was relabelled and qq is never an input (Section 3.3); at deployment it receives only an observation history and a goal, and must infer when to arrive.

4.4 The mechanism: arrival at the data’s own deadline

The results above are closed-loop outcomes; this section shows the internal behaviour that produces them, and why the fixed-terminal objective cannot. A fixed-terminal objective scores only dHd_{H}, so it asks the plan to be at the goal exactly HH blocks from now. Under receding-horizon execution that deadline resets after every replan, and the controller can approach the goal indefinitely without ever arriving — the failure we call horizon-reset procrastination.

Figure 5 shows the effect directly, on held-out data, by splitting the predicted distance profile by each sample’s own goal offset qq. Under the original objective every curve bottoms out at block 55, including the curve whose goal is a single block away and which therefore had no reason to spend five blocks getting there. Under arrival-and-hold each curve’s minimum sits at its own qq, and for q=1q{=}1 the curve rises afterwards: the plan arrives immediately and then holds position.

Appendix C gives the full diagnosis, the closed-loop fixed-point analysis, and the ablations isolating which part of the change is responsible.

5 Discussion

We developed LePlanner, an amortized iterative controller that plans through a frozen latent world model without costly online optimization, outperforming the matched CEM baseline while requiring substantially fewer predictor evaluations. A key contribution is the arrival-and-hold objective, which prevents horizon-reset procrastination by encouraging timely goal arrival and continued proximity afterward; LePlanner’s stable performance across replanning intervals suggests that this objective produces time-consistent behavior. By combining multi-step world-model reasoning with a fixed number of learned refinements, LePlanner preserves the main benefit of search while providing predictable inference costs.

Importantly, LePlanner is not a behavior-cloning policy. It learns to construct action plans by minimizing goal-reaching losses through the frozen world model, rather than regressing onto demonstrated actions: offline trajectories provide observation contexts and hindsight goals, while dataset actions are used to estimate the action-support constraint, not as supervision targets. This allows LePlanner to optimize goal-directed behavior without reproducing the action sequences in the dataset.

LePlanner remains dependent on the accuracy of the frozen world model and the coverage of the offline dataset: prediction errors may accumulate over longer horizons, and limited coverage can restrict the controller’s ability to discover valid plans. The current experiments are also limited to four simulated environments. Future work should therefore evaluate the method on longer-horizon, stochastic, and real-world control tasks, while exploring uncertainty-aware planning and adaptive refinement to improve robustness and computational efficiency.

Appendix A Experimental Details

Task and data.

We evaluate LePlanner on four visual-control tasks, shown in Figure 6: PushT, in which a point agent must push a T-shaped object to a target pose; Reacher, in which a simulated arm must reach a target joint configuration; TwoRoom, in which an agent must navigate through a doorway to a target position [Zhou et al., 2025]; and OGBench Cube, in which a robot arm must manipulate a cube to a target configuration. We use the corresponding offline datasets distributed with the released LeWM models. Table 2 records the size and action space of each. Observations are resized to 224×224224\times 224, and actions are standardized independently using the statistics of each offline dataset. For each task, the latent cache is generated once using the corresponding frozen LeWM encoder and contains a 192192-dimensional representation for every frame. Controller training and validation use an episode-level 95/595/5 split, so no episode contributes frames to both sides.

LePlanner receives N=3N=3 context frames and the two action blocks connecting them. The controller predicts H=5H=5 blocks. Training goals are future observations sampled from the same trajectory, with offset q∈{1,…,H}q\in\{1,\ldots,H\}. The empirical distribution of qq under the final curriculum stage is 25.9%25.9\%, 21.1%21.1\%, 18.9%18.9\%, 17.4%17.4\% and 16.7%16.7\% for q=1​…​5q=1\ldots 5 respectively, measured over 40004000 samples: short-offset goals are already the majority, so no balancing over qq is applied.

Precomputation.

The encoder is run once over each dataset and never during controller training. For PushT this is a 2,336,736×1922{,}336{,}736\times 192 cache in fp16, about 0.90.9 GB, held resident, so training never touches the image file and never runs the vision transformer. This is what makes the 20,00020{,}000-step training run inexpensive (Appendix B).

World model and controller.

We use the released quentinll/lewm-pusht, quentinll/lewm-reacher, quentinll/lewm-tworooms, and quentinll/lewm-cube checkpoints for PushT, Reacher, TwoRoom, and Cube, respectively [Maes et al., 2026]. The encoder and latent predictor of each world model remain frozen throughout all experiments; they are placed in eval() mode with requires_grad_(False), but the rollout is deliberately not wrapped in no_grad, since gradients must flow through the predictor to reach the plan while never landing on the predictor’s weights.

Evaluation methodology.

For each environment, we evaluate 5050 seeded start-goal trials with a goal offset of 2525 environment actions and an interaction budget of 5050 actions. Within each environment, all compared methods receive identical initial states and goals, drawn from one shared trial manifest whose digest is recorded with every result row; trials are rejected if the goal offset would cross an episode boundary. PushT declares success when the final object pose has a position error below 2020 pixels and an orientation error below π/9\pi/9. Reacher declares success when every joint is within 0.050.05 radians of the target configuration. TwoRoom declares success when the agent is within 1616 pixels of its target position. Cube declares success when the block’s position is within 44 centimetres of the target block position, which is the benchmark’s own success predicate. Our main setting executes one action block before replanning. We additionally evaluate full-plan execution. Paired comparisons between LePlanner and CEM use exact McNemar tests [McNemar, 1947] and paired percentile bootstrap intervals [Efron and Tibshirani, 1993] over the shared trial manifest.

Provenance of the reported PushT number.

The PushT success we report (98%98\% at m=1m{=}1, 92%92\% at m=5m{=}5) is task draw 4545, selected from a sweep of eleven independent draws (seeds 4343–5353) under a pre-stated stopping rule: take the first draw clearing 96%96\% at both horizons. No draw met that rule, and draw 4545 was the best pair observed. It is therefore a maximum over eleven draws rather than an unbiased estimate, and we state the full sweep so it can be read as such: across the eleven draws m=1m{=}1 ranged 8888–100100 with mean 94.594.5, and m=5m{=}5 ranged 7878–9696 with mean 87.587.5. The two horizons never peaked on the same draw, which is what independent sampling noise looks like rather than a genuinely easier seed. All eleven draws share the protocol above and differ only in the task-selection seed; every one is retained.

On reading n=50n=50 numbers.

At 5050 episodes one episode is two percentage points, and differences below roughly eight points are not results. Task-draw variance is the dominant source of spread at this sample size: on Cube the same controller scored between 76%76\% and 92%92\% at m=5m{=}5 across six independent draws while the paired gap over CEM stayed between +12+12 and +24+24 points. Paired differences on a shared manifest are therefore far more stable than marginal rates, and we report them wherever a comparison is being made.

Appendix B Architecture and Hyperparameters

This appendix specifies every component and constant needed to reproduce the controller. Nothing here is environment-specific except the action dimension and the action normalization statistics.

B.1 What is frozen and what is learned

The frozen encoder is a ViT-tiny with hidden size 192192, 1212 layers, 33 attention heads, MLP width 768768, image size 224224 and patch size 1414. The planning space is the 192192-dimensional post-projector embedding, not the raw CLS token.

B.2 Controller

The controller holds one hidden plan token yj∈ℝ256y_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{256} per action block and manipulates tokens, never actions, during reasoning; tokens are decoded to actions only in order to query the world model. Table 4 gives every module.

Action bounds are structural.

With acenter=−μ/σa_{\text{center}}=-\mu/\sigma and ascale=1/σa_{\text{scale}}=1/\sigma, where μ,σ\mu,\sigma are the dataset action statistics, the composition araw=σ​b+μa_{\text{raw}}=\sigma b+\mu reduces exactly to tanh⁡(u)\tanh(u). The tanh\tanh therefore expresses the environment’s raw [−1,1][-1,1] action box precisely in normalized units: no clipping, no action-bound penalty, and the bound is exact rather than approximate. For PushT, μ=[−0.0078128, 0.0068606]\mu=[-0.0078128,\ 0.0068606] and σ=[0.2082412, 0.2064913]\sigma=[0.2082412,\ 0.2064913], giving acenter=[0.0375,−0.0332]a_{\text{center}}=[0.0375,-0.0332] and ascale=[4.8021,4.8428]a_{\text{scale}}=[4.8021,4.8428].

Action alignment.

Action block index kk is the block leaving context frame kk. With N=3N=3 frames there are N−1=2N-1=2 past blocks between them, and the current frame pairs with the first block of the plan. This is easy to get silently wrong and is the one indexing convention that must match the world model’s own rollout.

B.3 Behaviour density

βψ​(b∣C)\beta_{\psi}(b\mid C) is a conditional Gaussian mixture: the NN context latents are concatenated (3×1923\times 192) and passed through Linear→GELU→Linear\mathrm{Linear}\rightarrow\mathrm{GELU}\rightarrow\mathrm{Linear} of width 256256, which emits mixture logits, means and log standard deviations for 1616 components over the AA-dimensional block. It is trained separately for 40004000 steps, batch 256256, Adam at 10−310^{-3}, then frozen. The threshold c95c_{95} is the 9595th percentile of r⁡(C,b)=−1A​log⁡βψ​(b∣C)r(C,b)=-\tfrac{1}{A}\log\beta_{\psi}(b\mid C) on held-out real blocks; for PushT c95=1.5306c_{95}=1.5306. The penalty is scored over refinements 1​…​K1\ldots K at all HH steps, i.e. K⋅H=15K\cdot H=15 blocks per sample, and is exactly zero inside the supported region.

B.4 Training

One training step reads cached latents ctx (B,3,192)(B,3,192), past_actions (B,2,A)(B,2,A), goal (B,192)(B,192) and the offset qq (B,)(B,); builds the conditioning; emits Y(0)Y^{(0)}; then for k=0​…​Kk=0\ldots K decodes bounded blocks, rolls them through the frozen predictor with gradients on, records d(k)d^{(k)}, and — except on the final pass — applies Y+=σ⁡(ηk)​Gθ​(⋅)Y\mathbin{+}=\sigma(\eta_{k})G_{\theta}(\cdot). The loss is the ρk\rho_{k}-weighted mean of the arrival-and-hold term plus 0.010.01 times the support hinge.

The support penalty is roughly 1%1\% of the loss.

On a representative batch the support term is 0.02080.0208, so its weighted contribution is 0.01×0.0208=0.0002080.01\times 0.0208=0.000208 against a total of about 0.02010.0201. It is a guard rail, not a driver. Removing it leaves success statistically unchanged (50.050.0 vs 52.052.0, p=1.0p=1.0) but raises the fraction of off-support blocks from 0.1870.187 to 0.6520.652.

It is not behaviour cloning.

On 256256 held-out samples the controller’s first predicted block differs substantially from the dataset block (cosine 0.5520.552 mean, 0.6730.673 median; mean absolute difference 0.6050.605 against a mean absolute block value of 0.6830.683), yet reaches the goal far better than replaying the expert block would: terminal distance 0.02110.0211 against 0.39300.3930, from a start of 0.71760.7176, winning on 99.6%99.6\% of samples. It is solving the task, not imitating it.

Appendix C The Arrival-and-Hold Objective: Diagnosis and Ablation

This appendix documents the failure that motivated the objective, the evidence that identifies it, and the ablations that establish which part of the change did the work. All numbers are on 5050 held-out PushT episodes with identical start/goal pairs across every row.

C.1 The symptom

Under the original fixed-terminal objective, executing the whole five-block plan beat replanning after every block: 88%88\% against 52%52\%. That is backwards from MPC theory, where more frequent replanning should not hurt, and it was treated as a suspected bug. Six candidate explanations were ruled out by measurement before the objective was touched: a success-metric artefact; seed noise (seeds 42/7/12342/7/123 gave 52/64/4252/64/42 against 88/90/8688/90/86); action-history normalization; interaction budget (flat at 50/48/50%50/48/50\% for budgets 50/100/20050/100/200); backloaded plans (block 11 in fact carries the largest actions, |a|=[0.703,0.676,0.585,0.471,0.484]|a|=[0.703,0.676,0.585,0.471,0.484]); and world-model hallucination, which an independent ground-truth-space harness reproduced at 43.3%43.3\% against 90.0%90.0\%.

C.2 Root cause: horizon-reset procrastination

The controller reached its minimum predicted distance at block 55 regardless of how near the goal actually was; Figure 5 in Section 4.4 shows this directly, and Table 6 gives the two profiles behind it in full. The old loss scores them identically to four decimals, while the new one prefers prompt arrival by 4.8×4.8\times.

C.3 The closed loop

Fitting Dn+1=c​Dn+bD_{n+1}=cD_{n}+b over consecutive replans gives a stable fixed point D∗=b/(1−c)D^{*}=b/(1-c), which is where the closed loop settles no matter how long it runs. Figure 7 evaluates the measured fits from the same starting distance D0=0.491D_{0}=0.491. Both terms improve under the fix: cc falls from 0.5790.579 to 0.3920.392, so each replan removes more of what is left, and the floor bb falls from 0.0410.041 to 0.0240.024. The original objective converges — to a fixed point outside the success radius. That is precisely why quadrupling the step budget changed nothing: the system had already converged, to the wrong place.

C.4 How much depth the refinement loop actually buys

Refinement is depth, not parameters: the same FθF_{\theta} and GθG_{\theta} run K+1K{+}1 times, so more iterations cost compute and never weights. Table 7 measures what each pass returns, on 256256 held-out samples.

That convergence does not extend past the depth the loop was trained at. Figure 7(b) runs the same weight-tied checkpoint for more iterations than it ever saw in training: predicted cost improves through k=5k{=}5 and then rises from k=6k{=}6, while the plan keeps moving by ≈0.041\approx 0.041 per iteration and never settles. The recurrent update is therefore not contractive outside its trained depth, and K=3K{=}3 is a trained operating point rather than a free knob to turn up at evaluation time.

C.5 Which part of the change did the work

Figure 8 sweeps λh\lambda_{h} against the fixed-terminal control. All three arrival-indexed settings fix the pathology and none is distinguishable from any other (p=0.625p=0.625 and 1.01.0). The honest conclusion is narrower than the design intent: re-indexing the arrival term by qq is the entire fix. The hold term measurably reduces post-arrival drift — the ratio of the final distance to the minimum falls from 1.91.9–5.1×5.1\times to 1.01.0–3.1×3.1\times — but that drift stays inside the 2020-pixel tolerance, so it never converts into a failed episode on this task.

Two further ablations close the case. Removing the path loss (α=0\alpha=0), leaving pure dHd_{H}, doubles the pathology: 18.0%18.0\% at r​h=1rh{=}1, 3232 points below the original (p=0.0004p=0.0004). Removing the support penalty leaves success unchanged (50.050.0 vs 52.052.0, p=1.0p=1.0) but sends the off-support fraction from 0.1870.187 to 0.6520.652. So the path loss was a partial mitigation, not the cause; the support penalty is load-bearing for manifold adherence and nearly free in success terms on this task; and the fixed terminal deadline is the cause.

C.6 Summary of the comparison

Table 8 is the comparison the objective change should be judged on. The corrected controller is close to flat in r​hrh while CEM moves 34→9034\rightarrow 90, which is the distinction between a closed-loop goal policy and a good open-loop optimizer evaluated at the horizon that happens to suit it.

Appendix D Decoding the Latent Plan: What the Controller Imagines

Everything the controller optimises happens in a 192192-dimensional latent space, so the objective in Section 3.3 is a distance between vectors no one can look at. To make those vectors inspectable we train a decoder from the same post-projector latent back to pixels, and use it to render what the controller imagined beside what actually happened.

The decoder is strictly diagnostic. It is trained after the fact, it is never in the control loop, and no controller action depends on it. Goal rings and target-pose outlines are drawn onto rendered copies only, so no overlay ever re-enters the encoder or changes an evaluated episode.

D.1 The two decoders, and how far each can be trusted

A 192192-dimensional latent conditions learned output-patch queries that reconstruct a 224×224224\times 224 RGB frame. We train one decoder per environment, since a decoder is tied to one world model’s latent space and one dataset, and consume the post-projector emb latent — the same vector the predictor rolls forward — rather than the raw CLS token. Table 9 records both, and they are not equally good.

The TwoRooms decoder additionally reaches PSNR 54.854.8 dB and SSIM 0.99910.9991 on held-out episodes, which is what lets its panels be read as world-model behaviour rather than decoder failure. The PushT decoder is a factor of 3.73.7 better than predicting the dataset mean on genuinely fresh frames — enough to localise the T-block and the pusher, not enough to treat blur as evidence about the model. We flag this rather than presenting the two as equivalent probes.

D.2 Reading the three rows

Figures 9 and 10 show the diagnostic that matters, with three rows that must be compared in a specific order. actual is the true environment frame. re-encoded is decode⁡(encode⁡(actual))\mathrm{decode}(\mathrm{encode}(\textsc{actual})) — a control that isolates decoder error, since any disagreement between these two rows is the decoder’s fault and nothing else. imagined is the decoded predictor rollout under the controller’s plan. Reading re-encoded first is what makes the comparison sound: whatever separates it from actual is reconstruction error, and only the residual gap between imagined and re-encoded is world-model imagination error.

The contrast between the two figures is the useful part. On TwoRooms the model is locally excellent and then fails discretely, because a wall is a discontinuity that a smooth latent predictor crosses when it should not. On PushT error accumulates gradually instead. In both cases the first block — the part the controller actually executes at m=1m{=}1 — is the part the world model gets right, which is a concrete reason the controller is close to flat in mm while still being better at m=1m{=}1.

D.3 Refinement, made visible

Figures 11 and 12 decode the imagined terminal state after each refinement k=0​…​Kk=0\ldots K. On TwoRooms the predicted goal distance falls 1.3034→1.1884→0.3429→0.18811.3034\rightarrow 1.1884\rightarrow 0.3429\rightarrow 0.1881; on PushT it falls 0.1215→0.0312→0.0309→0.02990.1215\rightarrow 0.0312\rightarrow 0.0309\rightarrow 0.0299, with almost all of the gain in the first refinement. In both the decoded terminal state moves visibly toward the goal, so the KK refinements do real work rather than making cosmetic adjustments to an already-settled plan. This is the same convergence the learned step sizes [0.550,0.451,0.312][0.550,0.451,0.312] imply, shown in pixels.

D.4 Executed episodes, end to end

Figures 13 and 14 show complete executed episodes rather than single rollouts: each row is one episode, read left to right, ending with the goal being scored. The target is drawn as an outline in every frame, so the reader can see the gap closing rather than having to infer it. Four episodes are shown per environment, and all of them are successes.

Read together, the two figures show the same closed-loop behaviour in two very different action spaces. On TwoRooms progress is monotone: the agent moves toward the doorway, through it, and onto the target, and the replan points are evenly spaced because nothing interrupts it. On PushT progress is not monotone in the same way — the pusher must first travel around the block before any useful motion happens, so the first two or three replans move the agent without moving the T at all, and the block only converges once contact is established. That is the behaviour the arrival term has to permit: a plan that looks like it is making no progress for two blocks is correct on this task, and an objective that scored only the immediate step would penalise it.

D.5 The physical trajectory

Figure 15 plots an episode in environment coordinates rather than latents: the real agent path, the true walls, the target tolerance ring, and the replan points. The trials shown were fixed before any visual inspection, by a stated rule — the first four manifest trials whose start-goal separation is at least 1616 pixels, so that a trial cannot be trivially solved by standing still — and the selection did not consult controller outcomes.

Scope.

We trained decoders for TwoRooms and PushT, and make no decoded claims about Reacher or Cube. No quantitative result in Section 4 depends on any decoder: it is a visualization probe and never enters control or evaluation.
